To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

heterogeneous genome divergence can be caused by either primary intergradation or secondary contact, and that patterns of genome divergence in hybrid zones are not necessarily concordant across transects or hybrid zones.

1) hybrid zones provide a window on the process of divergence and speciation; 2) heterogeneous genome divergence is common in natural populations; 3) heterogeneous genome divergence may arise as a result of differential introgression following hybridization or as a consequence of variation in selection or recombination; 4) the latter may be the predominant cause in some cases; 5) hybrid zone origins can be inferred by comparing the structure of hybrid zones with that of the parental populations; and

heterogeneous genome divergence can be caused by both primary intergradation (divergence in the absence of gene flow) and secondary contact (divergence with gene flow) and that the two processes cannot be distinguished by patterns of divergence in the absence of data on gene flow.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the origins, structure and dynamics of hybrid zones, with an emphasis on the role of heterogeneous divergence in the formation and maintenance of hybrid zones.
the origins of hybrid zones, and how they can inform us about the genetic architecture of reproductive barriers.
how the genetic structure of hybrid zones is determined and how this structure relates to the evolutionary process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
hybrid zones are windows on the evolutionary processes, but that these processes are highly complex and that the patterns observed are highly variable.
heterogeneous genome divergence, differential gene flow, and the origin of hybrid zones are all possible and that they can be difficult to distinguish.
heterogeneous genome divergence and restricted introgression are not mutually exclusive.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the origin and structure (i.e., width, location of contact zones, etc.) of hybrid zones is complex, and the genetics of hybridization is likely to be highly variable across taxa.
hybrid zones are indeed good windows on evolution, but that we are just now learning how to see through the glass.
heterogeneous genome divergence and differential introgression are the rule, rather than the exception, in hybrid zones.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the genetic architecture of reproductive barriers and local adaptation may vary substantially among hybrid zones and that the origin of a hybrid zone may not be apparent in a single transect.
heterogeneous genomic divergence is common in hybrid zones.
the origin of hybrid zones is not a simple matter of secondary contact between diverging populations.
